terms.Plans A-D (misalignment risk): Ryan Greenblatt (Redwood, October 2025) also defines Plan E, where almost no one with access cares. His subjective estimates of which world we are in are 5%, 10%, 25%, 45% and 15% for A-E, with takeover risks of 7%, 13%, 20%, 45% and 75% assuming competent execution. Lead time scales from about 10 years (A) to 1-3 years (B), 2-9 months (C) and roughly zero plus 10-30 insiders with about 3% of compute (D). His key implication is to focus substantially on C and D, and to avoid tactics that make lab staff dismissive of safety. Worlds can move between rungs as political will changes.
terms.Capability lead: Lead is measured in time to reach a capability, not in benchmark points: Epoch estimates Chinese models trail the US frontier by about 7 months on its capability index, while Aschenbrenner wanted a two-year lead to spend on safety. Leads can be eroded quickly by weight or algorithm theft, which is why security features so heavily in race arguments. Strategists disagree on whether pursuing a lead is stabilizing (room to slow down) or destabilizing (it may provoke rivals, per MAIM and RAND analyses). In Greenblatt's Plans A-D, the usable lead sets how much safety work and testing is possible before handoff to AI.
terms.Deferring to AI: Greenblatt and Stastny (Redwood, February 2026) argue deference may become unavoidable because control stops working at high capability and refusing to defer becomes uncompetitive. Requirements: the AI is not scheming, is aligned and well-elicited on hard-to-check open-ended tasks, has good epistemics, is capable at key tasks, stays corrigible and remains robust across long, massively parallel work. They recommend deferring to AIs only somewhat above top-human-expert level and building behavioral tests (analogies, work tests, exams, honeypots) that generalize to the deployed regime. They estimate over 90% success given a good initial AI and about one month of lead time.
terms.Basin of good deference: The concept mirrors the 'basin of corrigibility': a sufficiently good initial AI improves alignment and wisdom in each successor, so small errors shrink. The deference-goodness tax is the effort needed to stay in the basin relative to pure capability R&D; it could be near zero or exceed 100%, and lead time is what pays it. AIs inside the basin can also help buy time, partly offsetting the tax. The hard questions are how to tell, from behavioral evidence, whether an AI is inside the basin, and how to avoid overfitting to the tests used to decide.
terms.Mutual assured AI malfunction: Superintelligence Strategy pairs MAIM with nonproliferation (chip tracking, export controls, firmware security) and competitiveness (domestic chip supply). Oscar Delaney's December 2025 analysis splits the claim into three premises, giving roughly 70%, 60% and 60%, so about 25% that MAIM actually stops a unilateral US push, and distinguishes descriptive from normative MAIM. Critiques: no discrete red line as with nuclear use, uncertain Chinese threat perception, hardened or distributed compute undermining sabotage, and verification problems. MAIM advocates favor visible, remote datacenters; stability-focused analysts sometimes favor hardened ones, a real tension.
terms.Preventive attack: Burdette and Demelash (RAND, 2025) model preventive-war pressure through four variables: the expected power shift, the effectiveness and cost of preventive options, and whether leaders see conflict as inevitable. They find war unlikely in absolute terms but riskier when leaders are convinced AGI brings explosive growth and lasting first-mover advantage, and when they think limited force can stop the shift without general war. A counterintuitive result is that attacks look relatively likelier to preserve an AGI monopoly than to prevent one. Slow diffusion and dispersed, hardened infrastructure reduce pressure.
terms.Government AGI project: IAPS (Wildeford, Delaney, Anderson-Samways, November 2025) defines it by government control over starting, stopping and owning the final model, and estimates a median 34% that such a project produces the first AIR-10 system before 2035. Base rates from 35 past US innovations range from 23% (AI breakthroughs) to 78% (megaprojects). Arguments for: scale, security against state theft, a democratic chain of command. Arguments against: arms-race signaling, rushed safety, power concentration, slow government. IAPS recommends a 'minimum effective dose' of involvement: lab security standards, tracking rivals and contingency planning.
terms.Federal AI preemption: Preemption can be express (a statute says so), conflict-based, or field-based; executive orders cannot preempt on their own but can direct litigation and conditions on federal grants. The December 2025 order created a DOJ AI Litigation Task Force, ordered a Commerce review of state laws, conditioned some broadband funds, and asked the FCC and FTC to act, while proposing carve-outs for child safety, infrastructure and state procurement. Analysts at Carnegie doubt the FCC's authority. As of mid-2026, reporting indicated Congress had not enacted preemption, so laws such as SB 53 remained in force.
terms.Frontier safety framework: Frameworks differ in bindingness and scope. Anthropic's RSP v3.0 (2026) split unilateral commitments from industry-wide recommendations and added Risk Reports and a Frontier Safety Roadmap; OpenAI's Preparedness v2 (2025) uses High and Critical thresholds in three tracked categories; Google DeepMind's FSF v3 uses CCLs with alert thresholds and safety case reviews; xAI sets numeric benchmark bars; Meta stops development at critical risk. Most include a clause for relaxing safeguards if rivals do not match them. Critics stress self-grading and revisability; SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act now require publication and adherence to one's own framework.
terms.Export controls (AI chips): US controls since 2022 restrict advanced GPUs, high-bandwidth memory and chipmaking equipment such as advanced lithography, with policy shifting over time (for example, the 2025 back-and-forth on Nvidia's H20). The 2025 AI Action Plan proposed exploring chip location verification and closing gaps on equipment subsystems. Epoch's analysts note Huawei's Ascend 910C trails Nvidia's B200 by about 3x and that SMIC yields lag TSMC, yet Chinese models trail the frontier by only about 7 months, showing controls constrain compute more than capability. Smuggling, cloud access and stockpiling are known leaks.
